lesson.title: Chasing the Source: The Forced Response
lesson.summary: The forced response is the portion of a circuit's behavior driven entirely by the external source, the particular solution the circuit would settle into if given infinite time with that source connected. It supplies the steady-state target that the transient term decays toward.
lesson.body:
Every first-order circuit's full solution splits cleanly into two pieces that get added together: a natural response, which depends only on the circuit's own internal energy storage and dies away over time, and a forced response, which depends only on the external source and persists for as long as that source is connected. The forced response is sometimes called the particular solution, because in the language of differential equations it is the specific solution that satisfies the equation given the forcing function, as opposed to the general homogeneous solution that describes the circuit's unforced behavior.

For a constant (DC step) source, the forced response is identical to the steady-state response covered earlier: it is the value the circuit variable would reach and hold if you waited forever with the source connected as-is. That is because a constant forcing function eventually produces a constant output once the transient dies away, and the constant output is precisely the forced response. This is why the same open-capacitor, shorted-inductor technique used to find final conditions also finds the forced response; for step inputs they are computed the exact same way, just named for a different role in the solution.

Consider a series RL circuit where a 15 V source is switched on at t = 0, driving a 5 ohm resistor R1 in series with an inductor L, and that inductor is in parallel with a second resistor R2 = 10 ohms. To find the forced response of the inductor current, treat the inductor as a short circuit (its steady-state behavior with the source connected). A short circuit in parallel with R2 shorts out R2 entirely, so no current can flow through it; all the source current instead flows through the short, meaning it flows entirely through the inductor's branch. The forced current is therefore i_forced = V/R1 = 15 V / 5 ohms = 3 A, since R2 contributes nothing once it is bypassed by the short.

It is worth being precise about what the forced response is not: it is not necessarily the final value the circuit will actually reach if the source later changes again, and it is not the value at t = 0. It is specifically what the circuit variable equals in the long run under the present source condition, holding that source fixed. If the source were instead a sinusoid rather than a step, the forced response would not be a single number at all; it would be a sinusoid at the source frequency with some amplitude and phase, found using phasor analysis, the AC circuit analysis toolkit from earlier in the course, rather than the shorted-inductor DC trick used here.

This 3 A value is not the end of the story, only the target. The complete response of this same circuit still needs the natural response term, which captures how the inductor current transitions from wherever it started toward this 3 A forced value along an exponential curve set by the circuit's time constant. That is exactly the combination explored next under complete response.
